newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel confident of deal on German budget.
newsitem.headline: Waigel confident of deal on German budget.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Wednesday the centre-right coalition government was on the way to ending an lingering row and reach a compromise on the 1998 federal budget.

Disagreements over how to raise funds to fill widening budget deficits have strained ties within Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition of Christian Democrats (CDU), the Christian Social Union (CSU) and Free Democrats (FDP).
Coalition party leaders kept silent on the state of budget negotiations after fresh talks apparently failed to achieve a breakthrough.

"We are well on the way, even if difficult decisions are still ahead of us. I think we will do it," Waigel told reporters in Munich, adding that the goal of the coalition was to raise funds by privatisations and spending cuts.

Although Hermann Otto Solms, chief budget negotiator for junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP), said the talks were "good and promising," no details emerged from a morning meeting at Kohl's federal chancellery.

Coalition sources said a budget deal could only be achieved next week at the earliest, since Kohl and other top government officials will fly to the Group of Seven summit in the U.S. city of Denver this weekend.

One man staying behind is Waigel, who newspaper reports said will have his work cut out to close a huge 32 billion mark ($18.5 billion) gap in the 1998 budget. Waigel has pledged to meet the fiscal criteria governing European monetary union while accepting FDP demands not to raise taxes.
Newspapers said on Wednesday that progress was being made in horse-trading on the budget, with Waigel looking to dock around five billion marks from departmental budgets next year.

A further 25 billion marks will come from selling off state companies -- chiefly from further sales of Deutsche Telekom AG stock -- while the balance should come from cutting Christmas bonuses for civil servants and other benefits.
Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), Waigel's Bavarian-based Christian Social Union (CSU) and the FDP must hammer out a deal by July 10 so that a budget draft can be rubber-stamped on the following day.

By then, Waigel will also have to decide whether to impose a supplementary budget to deal with the more pressing problem of cutting state borrowing to the Maastricht treaty limit of three percent of gross domestic product this year.
Germany's central bank, the Bundesbank, warned on Wednesday in its monthly report that the combined federal, regional and municipal government deficit was likely to exceed plans.

"...the deficits of the federal, regional and municipal authorities will probably exceed the planned levels," the bank's report said. "The foreseeable decline in the deficits could therefore lag behind expectations."
Slack government receipts early in the year have resulted from changes to the tax system, but the Bundesbank said the picture should improve oover the course of the year.

The Bundesbank made no forecast for the budget deficit, but gave Waigel a few crumbs of comfort by saying that social security budgets should run a surplus this year after posting a 13 billion mark deficit in 1996.
